title: Charity shop donations: 70–90% never sell in stores
dek: Of clothing donated to charity shops, only 10–30% is actually sold to customers; the rest is mostly exported to second-hand markets in Kenya and elsewhere, and parts that can't be processed locally end up in landfills or are incinerated.
why: Neither study is mere common knowledge: pocket money reveals family power dynamics, charity shops reveal global waste shifting, and both are backed by concrete data and cases.
who: Anyone curious about family financial education, the second-hand economy, or the environmental cost of fast fashion—especially those who question whether consumption can be a form of doing good.
skip: Skip the father's personal anecdote about withholding pocket money and the research methodology details at the beginning; they don't affect understanding of the findings.

points.h: Pocket money is not one system but three parallel economic logics
points.body: Harris borrows sociologist Viviana Zelizer's framework for understanding household economics from the 1920s—entitlements (fixed allowances by age), payments (earnings from chores), and gifts (birthday and holiday money)—and adds her own category: enterprise (independent earning). Each operates independently, with no single model that fits all families.

points.h: Pocket money buys not just goods but moral scrutiny
points.body: Money never comes unconditional. Harris finds parents use pocket money as invisible behavior management. Beth learned the logic—more money if she hung out with approved friends. Jessica was cut off after using her travel fund for an Armani pair of jeans at TK Maxx. Children learn not just budgeting but how to navigate between money and parental moral expectations, and how to claim autonomy.

points.h: Before reselling secondhand clothes, a fifteen-year-old calculates cost of goods
points.body: These girls don't just pick up odd jobs—they run secondhand clothing businesses. They calculate before buying whether an item can be resold on secondhand platforms and at what price, then decide whether to purchase. Sometimes they profit. This lets them keep pace with trends and sustain the consumption cycle while treating their wardrobe and cash flow like a business.

points.h: Saving money is a point of pride that beats spending it
points.body: Rather than boast about buying expensive things, these girls brag about how little they spent—‘this cost only a few quid,’‘got three or four vintage pieces for five pounds.’ Frugality itself becomes an achievement worth mentioning. But Harris notes that her interviews were mainly with white middle-class girls, and this culture of ‘virtue through thrift’ carries class and gender markers that may not extend to all young people.

points.h: Charity shops should not be assumed to be good
points.body: Fitton began her research because she liked them, but for exactly that reason she asks harder: the modest shop on the corner, which looks harmless, actually sits within complex relationships between state and commerce. She observes two distinct types—city-center chains increasingly resemble boutiques, while suburban shops retain the old ‘browse and hunt for bargains’ character—and finds persistent pressure within the industry to professionalize charity retail.

points.h: In charity shops, customers often haggle up, not down
points.body: Fitton calls the unwritten rules that exist outside official policy and escape both headquarters and public view the ‘quiet economy.’ It has three parts: pricing negotiations—forbidden by headquarters but customers do it anyway, often raising the price because they think it's for charity; staff hierarchies—people on community service orders, released prisoners, and job seekers may work backstage; and the donation network that supplies the goods.

points.h: Donated clothes: fewer than 30% actually sell
points.body: The most striking finding: of clothing donated to charity shops, only 10–30% (per Andrew Brooks' Clothing Poverty) ever makes it onto shelves and is bought. This contradicts the Charity Retail Association's own claim that ‘up to 90% sells’—the gap exists because charities only report the donated goods as income; they're not required to disclose where those goods actually end up.

points.h: Unsold clothes are burned or buried in Kenya
points.body: Unsold clothing enters international secondhand trade networks and typically ends up in Kenya, Tanzania, and elsewhere. Local traders pick what they can resell. What remains—torn, stained, with missing buttons—cannot sell. It gets landfilled or burned. A 2022 Greenpeace report documented these clothes piled along Kenyan rivers, polluting water. More critically: the boom in secondhand buying has not cut demand for new clothes. Ellen MacArthur Foundation projects that by 2030, the climate impact of new clothing production will exceed the combined impact of international aviation and shipping.

terms.def: Fitton's term for the unwritten practices in charity shops that exist outside official policy and evade both headquarters oversight and public view.
Harris's framework for how teenagers receive money: regular allowances by age, wages from chores, gifts on occasions, and independent earnings respectively.
Bales of secondhand clothing exported to Kenya and other markets; documented in Greenpeace reports as a significant source of textile waste and water pollution.
